I am 61 years old, and I have worked these fields in Quzhou since I was a boy. I never went to school, so I cannot read the words on the fertilizer bags, but I can read the soil and the sky. My family has 6 mu of good flat land on the North China Plain, and I know every corner of it.

This year, like every year, I will grow winter wheat and summer maize. I do not know any other way that puts food on the table. In early October, after the National Day holiday, I will plough the fields deep and sow improved wheat seed that I buy from the agricultural supply store in town. The shopkeeper knows me; he gives me the same variety that the other old farmers in our village plant. For the wheat, I will spread compound fertilizer before sowing, and then I will top-dress with urea twice—once when the wheat turns green after winter, and again at jointing. Water is life here, so I will irrigate four times: before the winter freeze, at green-up, at jointing, and at heading. I will spray pesticides three times when the weeds and aphids appear. If the weather is fair, I expect to harvest about 450 kilograms per mu in early June.

The day after I cut the wheat, I will rotary-till the stubble quickly because the summer season is short. I will plant hybrid maize seed the same day or the next. I will put fertilizer in the rows at planting and side-dress once more when the plants are knee-high. I will irrigate twice—once if June is dry, and once at the big trumpet stage when the cobs are forming. I will spray twice for weeds and corn borer. The maize should give me about 550 kilograms per mu by late September.

I will not plant vegetables or strange new crops. I am old, my back hurts, and my children work in the city. The wheat gives us flour for noodles and buns, and the maize feeds our few chickens and sells for cash. The grain buyers come right to the village edge. This system has never failed me, and I am too old to gamble.
